analysis.one_liner: Trades public Oak Flat land in Arizona to a copper mining company for private conservation parcels.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing: introduced in March 2010 with zero cosponsors, it was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and died in subcommittee when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: Resolution Copper Mining, a joint venture of the mining giants Rio Tinto and BHP, wanted federal land in Arizona known as Oak Flat — about 2,406 acres in Pinal County that had been withdrawn from mining for decades — in exchange for parcels of its own private land in six Arizona counties. This bill would have ordered that swap once appraisals showed equal value, let the company begin exploratory drilling in the meantime, permanently protect the cliffs of Apache Leap and a parcel called The Pond from mining, add roughly 5,300 acres of the company's land to national forests and two national conservation areas, and hand some federal land to the town of Superior. The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee until the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiary would have been Resolution Copper Mining, LLC — a joint venture of Rio Tinto and BHP — which would have received roughly 2,406 acres of federally protected land in Pinal County outright, plus early authorization to drill exploratory holes under and on the Oak Flat Withdrawal Area. Secondary beneficiaries: the town of Superior, Arizona, which would gain the Fairview Cemetery and airport parcels; recreation users, who would get $1,250,000 in access and facility improvements; and conservation interests, who would gain about 5,300 acres added to national forests, the San Pedro Riparian National Conservation Area, and the Las Cienegas National Conservation Area.

how_it_helps.text: For Resolution Copper, the bill's central provision is a mandatory land exchange: if the company offers its private parcels and the Secretary finds the public interest well served, the Secretary 'shall convey' roughly 2,406 acres of Oak Flat in Pinal County — land the bill text shows was already withdrawn from the mining laws — to the company.

The bill lets Resolution Copper begin mineral exploration under and on the Oak Flat Withdrawal Area before the exchange, with the drill work limited to a single pad and no surface disturbance under the withdrawal — an early start on evaluating the deposit.

It locks in a 3-year appraisal: once the Secretary approves the final appraised value, no reappraisal is required for 3 years, and improvements the company makes before the exchange are excluded from the appraised value of the federal land.

The town of Superior would receive title to the Fairview Cemetery and airport parcels (paying fair market value, reduced by any donation value from the exchange), and Resolution Copper would pay $1,250,000 for recreation access improvements north of State Highway 60 and along Highway 177.

analysis.who_pays: The public would permanently lose Oak Flat — about 2,406 acres of national forest that includes a popular campground and a site sacred to Western Apache tribes — conveyed to a private company for mining, in return for land of equal appraised value elsewhere. Any value adjustment payment if production exceeded the appraisal's assumptions would go into a land-acquisition fund, but the conveyed land itself, and the copper under it (on which hardrock mining pays no federal royalty), would leave public hands for good.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public loses Oak Flat and its campground

drawbacks.text: The bill directs the Secretary to convey roughly 2,406 acres of Oak Flat — land the text shows was already withdrawn from mining and public land laws — to Resolution Copper, ending public and protected status over that parcel permanently once the exchange closes.

Once the appraisal is approved, the Secretary is not required to update it for 3 years, even as Copper Basin land values and copper prices move; and any improvements Resolution Copper makes before the exchange are excluded from the federal parcel's appraised value.

Tribal consultation is required before the public-interest decision, but the bill makes consultation a step in the process, not a condition that tribes can meet or reject — the Secretary can still approve the exchange over tribal objection.

The bill requires a single combined environmental review document covering both the exchange and the connected mine plan 'to the maximum extent practicable,' an approach supporters of the land called an effort to compress the review of one of the largest mining projects in the country.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The package has real positives: it would permanently protect Apache Leap and The Pond from mining, add roughly 5,300 acres to national forests and two national conservation areas, fund recreation improvements, and pay exchange costs and a value adjustment if production exceeds the appraisal assumption. But the center of the bill is a mandated transfer of land that has been off-limits to mining since the 1950s to a single company, with a 3-year freeze on updating the appraisal and a congressional timetable pushing the review to finish within 3 years. For the public, the trade is permanent: once conveyed, Oak Flat can be mined and its campground lost, while the protections given in return are narrow. Critics of this land exchange — including Apache tribes, for whom Oak Flat is a sacred site — have argued for years that no conservation acreage makes up for that loss, and tribes gained only a consultation requirement, not a veto.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with no cosponsors, the bill went from the House Natural Resources Committee to its public lands subcommittee on March 22, 2010, and nothing further ever happened before the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Ann Kirkpatrick introduced the Copper Basin Jobs Act on March 18, 2010; it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
On March 22, 2010, it was referred to the Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests and Public Lands — the last action ever taken on the bill.
The bill drew no cosponsors in the House.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote was ever scheduled before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, so the measure died without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, Oak Flat stayed federally protected public land through the end of the 111th Congress — a win for tribes, recreation users, and anyone who wanted the land kept off the mining rolls. Resolution Copper simply lost two years; the same land exchange was pushed again in later Congresses and eventually passed in 2014.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oak Flat stayed public land; tribes and recreation users

for.name: Rep. Ann Kirkpatrick
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Copper Basin Jobs Act on March 18, 2010, and was its only sponsor.

for.name: Resolution Copper Mining, LLC (Rio Tinto and BHP joint venture)
for.role: Mining company seeking the Oak Flat land exchange
for.what_they_did: Sought the federal-to-private land exchange at the center of the bill and had pushed versions of it in Congress since 2005.

against.name: San Carlos Apache Tribe and other Western Apache tribes
against.role: Tribal governments for whom Oak Flat is a sacred ceremonial site
against.what_they_did: Opposed any transfer of Oak Flat out of federal protection; the bill's only concession to them was a required government-to-government consultation before the exchange decision, with no power to stop it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so its support was never measured on the floor or in committee.

industries.industry: Copper mining (Resolution Copper Mining, LLC — a joint venture of Rio Tinto and BHP)
industries.note: The bill mandates conveyance of about 2,406 acres of federal land withdrawn from mining since the 1950s — Oak Flat, which sits atop one of the largest undeveloped copper deposits in North America — to this one company, and lets it start drilling before the exchange. Because hardrock mining on public land in the U.S. pays no federal royalty, the copper beneath would be extracted essentially royalty-free.

Recreation users would gain about $1.25 million for trails, roads, and parking near Highway 60 and 177 and roughly 5,300 acres of new protected land — but would permanently lose the Oak Flat Campground and a longtime recreation area when it is conveyed to the mining company.

The town would receive the Fairview Cemetery and about 515 acres tied to the Superior Airport, paying fair market value reduced by the donation value from the exchange — a local government benefit wrapped around the company's land deal.
